The layout set on the computer you are controlling, not the one on this phone. Bluetooth sends key positions rather than characters, so this has to match the host or letters and punctuation come out swapped. Chinese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic, Thai and Vietnamese hosts use US QWERTY and compose their script themselves.

KuneLab Kontroller turns this phone into a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse. The host sees an ordinary Bluetooth keyboard, so nothing needs installing on it.

1. Leave this app open and allow the “make discoverable” prompt.
2. On the host, scan for Bluetooth devices and pair with this phone.
3. Confirm the passkey on both sides.

Afterwards, leave “Connect automatically” on in Settings and the phone will open the connection itself whenever you open the app.

• Move pointer: drag one finger
• Left click: tap, or the Left click button
• Right click: the Right click button
• Double click: double tap
• Drag and drop: hold a click button and drag on the pad
• Scroll: drag two fingers

A two-finger tap is also a right click: put both fingers down and lift them again without sliding.

Tap the keyboard icon to bring up the soft keyboard; whatever you type is sent to the host.

The (N)/(P) button controls modifier keys. (N) releases Ctrl/Alt/Shift after each keystroke; (P) holds them down so you can build combinations such as Ctrl held while clicking. Remember to switch back to (N), or modifiers stay stuck.

Gboard has no Ctrl, Esc, arrows or function keys. A keyboard app that does (Unexpected Keyboard or Hacker’s Keyboard) makes shortcuts such as Shift+F10 (context menu) possible.

With “Keep trying to reconnect” on, opening the app or tapping the host under Devices keeps calling it for up to a minute, the same way a Bluetooth mouse wakes a PC when you click it. The action bar shows the attempts while it tries.

Whether the host actually wakes is up to the host, and not every one can:

• Windows and Mac normally can already.
• On Linux the adapter has to be armed as a wake source by hand, and some adapters cannot do it at all. Intel chips are the safest bet; Realtek ones often lack the firmware support, in which case no setting will fix it.
• A machine that is hibernated or switched off can never be woken this way. Its Bluetooth radio has no power, and a real Bluetooth mouse cannot wake it either.

This has nothing to do with which desktop the host runs. GNOME, KDE or none at all makes no difference. While the machine is asleep the wake is handled by the Bluetooth chip and the kernel, long before any desktop exists.

If your host turns out not to wake, retrying is still worth leaving on: after you wake the machine yourself, the phone reconnects on its own instead of leaving you to reconnect it by hand.

If tapping a device under Devices does nothing, and Connect does nothing either, the phone's Bluetooth stack is most likely stuck.

Android allows only one app at a time to act as a Bluetooth keyboard. If a previous run was killed without disconnecting (it crashed, was force-stopped, or was reinstalled while connected), the stack keeps holding that dead registration and quietly refuses every new connection. The app cannot clear this itself.

Turn Bluetooth off, wait a few seconds, turn it back on, then reopen this app. That releases the stale registration and connecting works again.

If the app notices this has happened it will offer the same advice in a dialog.
If the host sees no keyboard

On Linux, a plain “connect” often brings up audio profiles instead of the keyboard. Either rely on “Connect automatically” so the phone initiates, or connect the HID profile explicitly:

bluetoothctl connect <MAC> 00001124-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb

If the host still shows no keyboard, BlueZ may have cached a service list from before this app registered. Remove the cache file for this phone under /var/lib/bluetooth and reconnect; the pairing itself survives.
